e.etymology: The Spanish and Italian form of a Visigothic name, usually explained as adal (noble) plus funs (ready). Many kings of Leon, Castile, Aragon and Spain bore it.
namesakes: Alfonso Ribeiro (Carlton on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air)
Alfonso Cuaron (director of Gravity and Roma)
Alfonso Soriano (baseball All-Star)

e.etymology: The Greek form of the Egyptian name Usir, borne by the god of the dead, the afterlife and rebirth. The meaning of the Egyptian name is not settled.

assoc.t: Egyptian god of the dead and the afterlife

e.etymology: The Italian form of the Latin name Maximus, from maximus (greatest), the superlative of magnus (great).
The Spanish form of Augustine, from Latin Augustinus, a derivative of Augustus (venerable). Saint Augustine of Hippo made the name widespread. Spanish spells it with an accent on the i.
A modern name used mostly in Mexican and Mexican American families. It carries the -beth ending of Lizbeth and Elizabeth; the first part has no settled source.
From a Norman surname taken from a place in Normandy, Old French for Gomeric's hill. Gomeric was a Germanic personal name built from words for man and ruler.
namesakes: Montgomery Clift (1950s film star)
Montgomery Burns (Mr. Burns on The Simpsons)
Montgomery Scott (Scotty in Star Trek)

e.etymology: From a surname with Irish and Scottish roots, tied to Gaelic cuilinn (holly); the Irish family name O Cuilinn means descendant of Cuileann. It rose as a first name with the Cullen family of Twilight.

assoc.t: Edward Cullen and his vampire family in Twilight

e.etymology: From Arabic khalid (eternal, immortal, glorious), the active participle of the verb khalada, to last forever. Khalid ibn al-Walid was a celebrated general of early Islam.
namesakes: Khalid (R&B singer of Location and Talk)

assoc.t: Khalid, the R&B singer who goes by the single name

e.etymology: A respelling of Ava. Ava is usually taken as a form of Eve, from the Hebrew for life; a separate medieval Germanic name Ava also existed.
A modern American name that adds the -lee ending to May, or reworks Miley and Mylee. May began as a pet form of Mary and Margaret and is also the month, named for the Roman goddess Maia.

e.meaning: one who works on a ship
e.etymology: The English word for a seafarer, taken up as a given name in the 2000s. The related surname Saylor comes instead from an Old French word for a dancer or acrobat.

assoc.t: Sailor Moon, the Japanese anime heroine

e.meaning: pet form of Matilda (mighty in battle) or Martha (lady)
e.etymology: A pet form of Matilda and Martha, and sometimes a variant of Maddie, that was given as a full name in the 19th-century United States. Matilda comes from Germanic words for might and battle.
namesakes: Mattie Ross (the girl who narrates True Grit)

e.etymology: From a Scottish surname that goes back to the Old Irish name Blaan, from bla (yellow), borne by a 6th-century saint. American use as a first name took off when James G. Blaine ran for president in 1884.
namesakes: Blaine Anderson (Darren Criss's character on Glee)

e.meaning: uncertain; often linked to Latin cor, heart
e.etymology: Shakespeare's spelling, in King Lear, of the legendary British queen Cordeilla. The source is unsettled: it may come from the Latin saint's name Cordula and is popularly tied to cor (heart).
namesakes: Cordelia (King Lear's loyal youngest daughter)
Cordelia Chase (Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Angel)

assoc.t: loyal youngest daughter in Shakespeare's King Lear

e.etymology: From a surname for someone who lived by a stream, from Old Norse bekkr and its German cognate; the German surname can also be a form of Becker (baker). As a first name it also serves as a short form of Beckett.
namesakes: Beck (musician behind Loser and Morning Phase)

e.etymology: From Late Latin Mauritius, derived from Maurus (Moor; dark, swarthy). A 3rd-century Roman soldier martyr, Saint Maurice, made the name popular, and it came into English through French.
namesakes: Maurice Sendak (author of Where the Wild Things Are)
Maurice White (founder of Earth, Wind & Fire)
Maurice Gibb (member of the Bee Gees)

e.etymology: A Latinized form of Evelyn, which goes back through the Norman name Aveline to the Germanic name Avila. Fanny Burney's 1778 novel Evelina made it familiar; it is often read as an elaboration of Eva.
A respelling of Beau, the French word for handsome, which became an English nickname and then a given name. Beaux is the plural of the word in French.
The French form of Corinna, from Ancient Greek kore (girl, maiden). Madame de Stael's novel Corinne, or Italy spread the name in the early 1800s.
namesakes: Corinne Bailey Rae (singer of Put Your Records On)

e.etymology: From a Scottish surname that began as a byname for a Welshman or Breton, from Anglo-Norman waleis (foreign). It became a first name in the 19th century in honor of the Scottish patriot William Wallace.
namesakes: Wallace Shawn (actor in The Princess Bride)
Wallace Stevens (American poet)

assoc.t: Wallace, the inventor in Wallace and Gromit
William Wallace, the Scottish hero of Braveheart

e.etymology: A modern respelling of Case, an English surname used as a first name and a clipped form of Casey. Kase is separately a German surname from the word for cheese.

e.meaning: son of Col, a medieval short form of Nicholas
e.etymology: A respelling of Colson, an English surname meaning son of Col or Cole, medieval short forms of Nicholas. It follows the fashion for names like Colton and Jensen.
The Spanish and Portuguese word for life, from Latin vita. Vida is also an old short form of Davida, a Slovene feminine of Vid (Vitus) and a Lithuanian name.
namesakes: Vida Blue (Cy Young Award-winning pitcher)

e.etymology: From Arabic kabir (big, great), which reached India through Persian. It is closely tied to Kabir, the 15th-century Indian mystic poet revered by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs.
The English name of the evergreen tree, from Latin cedrus and Greek kedros. It joined the given-name pool in recent decades with other tree names such as Aspen and Rowan.
A modern name with no settled origin. It follows the sound of Myra, Kyra and Lyra.
The Latin feminine of Marcellus, a Roman family name formed as a diminutive of Marcus, which is probably linked to the god Mars. Saint Marcella was a 4th-century Roman widow.
From a merger of Old English Hereweald and Old Norse Haraldr, both from Germanic words for army and ruler. Harold II, the last Anglo-Saxon king of England, fell at Hastings in 1066.
namesakes: Harold Ramis (Ghostbusters actor and Groundhog Day director)
Harold (boy hero of Harold and the Purple Crayon)
Harold Lloyd (silent film comedian)

assoc.t: Harold of Harold and the Purple Crayon

e.etymology: From Hebrew malka (queen), the feminine of melekh (king). It is a traditional name among Ashkenazi Jews and is common in Orthodox communities today.

e.meaning: a name of the goddess Sita
e.etymology: In India, Siya is a Hindi form of Sita, the wife of Rama in the Ramayana, whose Sanskrit name means furrow. In South Africa, Siya is a short form of Zulu and Xhosa names such as Siyabonga.
e.note: Sounds the same as the casual goodbye see ya.

e.etymology: From Hebrew Avner, built from av (father) and ner (lamp, light). In the Bible Abner is King Saul's cousin and the commander of his army.
namesakes: Abner Doubleday (Civil War general long credited with inventing baseball)
Li'l Abner (hillbilly hero of the classic comic strip)

e.etymology: The Hebrew and Yiddish form of Samuel, the biblical prophet and judge. It combines shem (name) and El (God); tradition, following the Bible's own account, reads it as God has heard.
